title: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations, Inc. v. Camp
shortTitle: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations, Inc. v. Camp
summary: Data-processing competitors could obtain judicial review of a ruling authorizing banks to provide competing services because they alleged economic injury and fell arguably within the relevant statutes’ zone of interests.

sections.Parties: The petitioners sold data-processing services to businesses. They sued the Comptroller of the Currency, who had issued the challenged ruling, and American National Bank & Trust Company, a bank allegedly competing for customers. The bank and Comptroller defended the authority of national banks to provide the services.
sections.Material Facts: The Comptroller’s 1966 ruling permitted a national bank, incidentally to its banking services, to make its data-processing equipment or services available to other banks and bank customers. The petitioners alleged prospective lost profits and identified two customers for whom Data Systems had agreed or negotiated to provide services that the bank was performing or preparing to perform. Those allegations supplied a concrete competitive injury. The challengers invoked the Bank Service Corporation Act and National Bank Act, including a restriction limiting bank service corporations to bank services for banks.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the complaint for lack of standing. The court of appeals applied a framework requiring a protected legal interest or a recognized public-interest basis for review. On Supreme Court review, the decisive threshold was whether these competitors were entitled to contest the Comptroller’s action. The assigned excerpt presents the Court’s rejection of the lower court’s legal-interest approach but omits the formal concluding judgment and subsequent proceedings.
sections.Issue: Whether data-processing businesses challenging bank competition must establish a protected legal right at the threshold, or instead have standing by alleging injury in fact and an interest arguably within the zone protected or regulated by the relevant statutes.
sections.Holding: The competitors satisfied the stated threshold. They alleged economic injury and asserted interests arguably within the relevant statutory zone, making them aggrieved persons entitled to judicial review under APA §702. The decision did not itself establish that the Comptroller’s ruling was unlawful or award relief on the merits.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Douglas separated the existence of a protected legal interest, which could depend on the merits, from the threshold ability to seek review. The alleged loss of business established injury in fact. The statutes’ restrictions on banks’ activities supplied an arguable relationship between the statutory scheme and competitors’ economic interests even though the statutes did not expressly designate the petitioners as beneficiaries. The Court also recognized that aesthetic, recreational, conservation, and other noneconomic interests could support review in appropriate circumstances. The casebook treats the opinion’s historical innovation critically: neither the phrase injury in fact nor the zone-of-interests formula appears expressly in §702, and the doctrinal move could broaden some APA suits while narrowing other public actions. That editorial critique concerns the test’s grounding and consequences; it does not alter the opinion’s conclusion that these plaintiffs could obtain review.
